Uncorruptible
un-ko-RUP-ti-bl
adj. (incapable of decay; imperishable)
Greek aphthartos, not liable to corruption or decay. The Authorized Version uses the form uncorruptible once, at Romans 1:23, and incorruptible elsewhere; Webster (1828) carries the entry under INCORRUPTIBLE.

Biblical Definition

And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things. Paul is describing the root of idolatry, and he describes it as an exchange. The word uncorruptible is doing the heavy work: it names what God is and what no creature is. He is not liable to decay, not subject to time, not running down — the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever, the King eternal, immortal, invisible. To worship him is to worship the one thing in the universe that cannot perish. Idolatry reverses the transaction with perfect and terrible symmetry: the uncorruptible is traded for the corruptible, and Paul walks the exchange down the ladder rung by rung — man, then birds, then fourfooted beasts, then creeping things. That descent is the argument. Idolatry never holds its level; having let go of the imperishable it slides, because there is no floor under it. The preceding verse gives the verdict on the trade: professing themselves to be wise, they became fools. And the psalmist supplies the plain fact the idolater will not face — their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands. The thing worshipped decays, and the worshipper with it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), under INCORRUPTIBLE: that cannot corrupt or decay; not admitting of corruption; incapable of being bribed or perverted.

expand to see more

INCORRUPTIBLE, a. That cannot corrupt or decay; not admitting of corruption.

INCORRUPTIBLE, a. That cannot be bribed; inflexibly just and upright.

CORRUPTIBLE, a. That may be corrupted; that may decay and perish; subject to decay and destruction.

IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.

IMMORTAL, a. Having no principle of alteration or corruption; exempt from liability to death; imperishable.

Key Scripture

Romans 1:23 — "And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things."

1 Timothy 1:17 — "Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen."

Psalm 115:4 — "Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands."

Colossians 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

Modern Corruption

Divine incorruptibility is quietly surrendered wherever God is made to change, suffer alteration, or develop with his creation; and idolatry is redefined as a matter of priorities rather than an exchange of glory.

expand to see more

Process theology denies divine immutability outright, and open theism, following Pinnock, Boyd, and Sanders, denies exhaustive foreknowledge and makes God a learner within time. Both are departures from Romans 1:23, which does not merely say God has not decayed but that he is uncorruptible — incapable of it by nature. The classical attributes are not Greek intrusions into Hebrew religion, as the standard objection runs; they are the plain entailment of the divine name and are asserted here by an apostle in the course of an argument about idolatry. A God who can be altered is a God who can be traded for, and the whole force of Paul's indictment collapses.

The second corruption softens idolatry into disordered priorities — whatever a man cares about most. There is a truth buried in it, but the flattening loses Paul's point. He describes an exchange of glory: a deliberate substitution of the corruptible for the uncorruptible in the place of worship. That is why the ladder descends to creeping things and why the chapter follows with God giving men up. Idolatry is not a ranking problem to be adjusted; it is treason against the only imperishable One, and the remedy is not better priorities but repentance.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek aphthartos (G862), incorruptible; phthartos (G5349), corruptible; allasso (G236), to change or exchange; doxa (G1391), glory.

expand to see more

Greek aphthartos (G862) — not liable to corruption or decay; rendered uncorruptible here, incorruptible elsewhere.

Greek phthartos (G5349) — corruptible, perishable; what man is, and what he traded for.

Greek allasso (G236) — to change, to exchange one thing for another; the verb of the idolatrous trade.

Greek homoioma (G3667) — a likeness, a resemblance; the image made like to of the descent.

Greek aphthartos at 1 Timothy 1:17 — the same divine incorruptibility doxologically confessed.

Usage

"“the glory of the uncorruptible God” — what was given up in the exchange."

"“into an image made like to corruptible man” — what was taken in its place."

"“birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things” — the descent idolatry never arrests."
